title: The 12 Leverage Points

tactic.name: Adopt Your Agent's Perspective
tactic.one_liner: Your agent is brilliant, but blind — ephemeral, context-free, reset to zero after every session — so hand it the information, tools, and resources YOU would use, and ask before every launch: with my agent's core four, can it complete the task I've given it?
tactic.why_uncomfortable: It inverts the engineer's self-image: 'It's not about you anymore. It's about what you can do for your agent so they can work for you.' Instead of being the one who solves the problem, you become the one who sets up the system so a blank-slate agent can solve it — including letting go of watching every step (YOLO mode now, programmable mode from lesson 3 on). Dan names the discomfort directly: engineers love control and visibility, and the hardest thing in TAC is letting that go.

mission: Give you a framework that won't change over time (the compressed phase-two SDLC: plan, code, test, review, document) plus a tactic (adopt your agent's perspective) and a checklist (the 12 leverage points) so you can maximize not what you can do, but what your agents can do — measured by four KPIs: size up, attempts down, streak up, presence down. All of it in service of the TAC mission: becoming the irreplaceable engineer whose codebase increasingly runs itself.

sdlc_phase2.why: Tools, models, and compute churn; the software development lifecycle is an aspect of engineering that never changes — 'you can place big bets on it.' TAC uses these five steps as the framework for success and spends the remaining lessons augmenting and automating them so 'your agent ships on your behalf.'

in_agent.definition: The core four — 'in the agent because they're always with your agent.' On the lesson slide: Context = system prompts and conversation history; Model = LLM selection and configuration; Prompt = user instructions and queries; Tools = available functions and capabilities.

through_agent.definition: 'External levers that eventually interact with your agent that have massive impact on your success. They typically flow through the context window.' On the lesson slide: Standard Out = response from commands and logging; Types = types, schemas, classes, errors, and structures; Documentation = 3rd party and internal; Tests = self-validating feedback loops; Architecture = codebase structure; Plans = detailed prompts for massive work; Templates = reusable, embeddable, agentic prompts; ADWs = AI Developer Workflows.

leverage_points.count_check: 4 in-agent + 8 through-agent = the 12 leverage points of agentic coding.

kpis.size: Increase. The amount of work handed off per prompt — bigger plans, longer agent runs. Five-minute agentic jobs are good; push toward 10, 20, 30 minutes, an hour, three hours. 'Don't underestimate the amount of work you can hand off autonomously.'
kpis.attempts: Decrease (toward one per prompt). Every post-completion correction costs 'your most important engineering resource: your time.' Attempts of 5–10 (even 3–6) mean a leverage point is missing — find and employ it. Iterating is fine for exploratory work but is not the destination: 'We're not aiming to become a babysitter for AI agents. We're looking for one-shot solutions.'
kpis.streak: Increase. Back-to-back one-shot successes — streaks of 3, 5, 10. Five one-shot prompts that ship features drastically outperform five prompts needing three fixes each ('that's 3x slower'). 'Once you start one-shotting, don't break the streak' — and when it breaks, identify which leverage point was missing.
kpis.presence: Decrease (toward zero) — 'likely the most important.' Presence measures how much you must sit, guide, and correct your agent. Back-and-forth prompting is 'not the end game. This is the early game.' The balancing act: learn what runs at full autonomy (knob at 11) vs where you must still intervene.

core_concepts.name: Bet on what never changes: the phase-two SDLC
core_concepts.plain_english: Amid tool/model churn, Dan bets the course on the software development lifecycle, compressed to five steps — plan, code, test, review, document — as the framework TAC will augment and automate lesson by lesson until the codebase ships on your behalf.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Some aspects of engineering never change... you can place big bets on them... Plan, code, test, review, document. Over the next seven lessons, we're going to augment and automate key steps so that your agent ships on your behalf."
core_concepts.misconception: That the SDLC section is throat-clearing before the real content. Several leverage points ARE SDLC nodes (plans, tests, documentation) — Dan closes by pointing this out; missing the mapping turns a system into a trivia list.

core_concepts.name: Tactic #2: Adopt Your Agent's Perspective
core_concepts.plain_english: Agents boot as blank instances — no context, no memories, no awareness beyond what you provide — and reset to zero when done. To get engineer-grade work, hand the agent your perspective: the information, tools, and resources you would use. Litmus question from the tactic card: with my agent's core four, is it possible to complete the task I've given it?
core_concepts.dan_words: "Your agent is brilliant, but blind... Agents are ephemeral, no context, no memories, and no awareness outside of what you give it... Your agent needs your context, your model, your prompt, and your tools, the core four... It's not about what you can do anymore. It's about what you can teach your agents to do."
core_concepts.misconception: Assuming session continuity — that the agent 'remembers' the last session, the open browser, or the error on your screen. Anything not in the context window does not exist; /prime exists precisely because of this.

core_concepts.name: The 12 leverage points: in-agent vs through-agent
core_concepts.plain_english: Two families: the core four live IN the agent (context, model, prompt, tools); eight more levers work THROUGH the agent, flowing into the context window (standard out, types, documentation, tests, architecture, plans, templates, ADWs). Stack them and one-shot success becomes inevitable.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There are two types of leverage points: in agent and through agent... Through agents are external levers that eventually interact with your agent that have massive impact on your success. They typically flow through the context window... When you stack up these leverage points, Agentic Coding success becomes inevitable."
core_concepts.misconception: Memorizing the list without the diagnostic. The KPI section's drill is the point: when a run fails or a streak breaks, name WHICH leverage point was missing (dicts instead of types? no stdout? no tests? no plan?) and employ it.

core_concepts.name: Know your agent's tools (or forfeit them)
core_concepts.plain_english: Claude Code's tools live in its system prompt, so you can just ask (/tools) for the full list with parameters. Reading tool definitions surfaces exploitable details — like Bash's timeout parameter, which later lets Dan run a live server inside the agent for 300 seconds. The toolset CRUDs a codebase just like an engineer.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We need to see what our agents can see. We need to know what they can do... did you know that the bash tool here has a timeout?... There are many little hidden kind of secrets inside of every single tool... They can crud — create, read, update, delete — a codebase just like you and I can."
core_concepts.misconception: Never reading tool definitions, then under-using the agent (babysitting terminals outside it) or misreading its behavior (not knowing Task fires a subagent makes the type-trace demo look like magic). MCP servers extend the toolset later — the introspection habit is what transfers.

core_concepts.name: Standard out: your agent can only see what you let it see
core_concepts.plain_english: Stdout is the agent's window into runtime behavior — every command response, error, and log line. The demo app's server swallowed all exceptions into response fields with zero terminal trace: fine-ish for humans watching the browser, invisible to agents. That's bad agentic code.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Your agent can only see what you let it see. Standard out is the response from any command you run... clear logging throughout your applications, your commands and your scripts can guide your agent to success... Not only do we have bad code, we have bad agentic code."
core_concepts.misconception: Logging for humans (UI toasts, dashboards, external log services) instead of for agents (stdout/files the agent process can read). Also: fearing stdout overload — Dan gives three escape hatches (per-session log file, cleaned-up logs, warn/error levels) while insisting fuller output shrinks the state space the agent must search.

core_concepts.name: Set up the codebase so the agent fixes the bug
core_concepts.plain_english: Dan knows the CSV bug and deliberately does not fix it. Instead he (1) has the agent add [ERROR]/[SUCCESS] prints to every endpoint, (2) runs the server INSIDE a fresh agent via Bash timeout (sh ./scripts/start.sh, 300s), (3) reproduces the error, then asks 'any issues with the server?' — the agent cites file_processor.py:26 and the unsanitized parentheses — and (4) says 'resolve: replace bad chars and escape.' Two short prompts fix it because the system was set up first.
core_concepts.dan_words: "I'm not actually fixing the issue. I'm setting up my codebase so that my agent can resolve the issue... We're updating our codebase to communicate information to our agent... Are you still manually looking at error messages? Stop... Give them to your agent."
core_concepts.misconception: Hand-fixing the planted bug (you get a working app and learn nothing), or prompting 'fix the upload bug' BEFORE stdout exists and concluding agents can't debug — when the actual failure was a missing leverage point.

core_concepts.name: Types are IDKs (information dense keywords)
core_concepts.plain_english: Types — classes, exceptions, interfaces, all typing structures — create a traceable flow of information through a codebase. Copy DatabaseSchemaResponse into a context-free agent and ask how it flows: a Task subagent (7 tool uses, 26.7k tokens) returns the exact five-file path from Pydantic model to FastAPI endpoint to mirrored TS interface to API client to the original spec.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Types tell a story about how information travels throughout your codebase... Remember that types are IDKs, information dense keywords. They point to exact locations in your code base and represent the flow of a specific type of information."
core_concepts.misconception: Generic names kill the lever: QueryRequest/QueryResponse are 'not that good'; a name like DataRequest is 'terrible' — 'if your agent ever wants to search for data or just request, it's cooked.' Dict-passing codebases have no types to trace at all — the first problem→lever mapping in the KPI drill.

core_concepts.name: Architecture and the agent navigation problem
core_concepts.plain_english: Every fresh agent must re-explore your codebase — hundreds and thousands of boots. Structure is therefore a multiplier: the app/client vs app/server split alone halves the search space. Consistency (same patterns, folders, names, comment structure) is the antidote to complexity; a checklist of concrete practices makes codebases token-efficient and navigable.
core_concepts.dan_words: "I've called this the agent navigation problem. Every time you boot up a new agent, it has to explore the codebase... If it's hard for you, you should assume it'll be hard for your agent... consistency is a powerful actor against complexity for both humans and for agents."
core_concepts.misconception: Either ignoring architecture ('the agent will figure it out' — it will, expensively, every boot) or immediately hand-refactoring everything — Dan says 'don't refactor yet': future lessons organize agentic assets WITH your agent.

core_concepts.name: Documentation: internal + external, with ai_docs local-first
core_concepts.plain_english: Internal docs (README, agent-facing markdown spread through the tree) ramp fresh agents; external docs live in ai_docs/ — a folder dedicated to agents holding third-party references (OpenAI/Anthropic quickstarts here) so agents don't burn time and tokens on web requests mid-task.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There are two types, internal documentation and external documentation. AI docs is a dedicated folder specifically for our agents. You don't want them making web requests every time they have to look something up. Just get it local."
core_concepts.misconception: Looking for a CLAUDE.md in tac-2 — Dan name-checks the convention, but this repo ships none; README.md + /prime carry the role here. Also assuming the agent 'knows' current APIs from training — the whole point of vendoring quickstarts locally is drift-free, in-context reference.

core_concepts.name: Tests: self-validating feedback loops
core_concepts.plain_english: Agents will make mistakes; tests are the leverage that lets them catch and correct their own. Run pytest inside the agent (bash mode) and the full output feeds the context window — a closed loop where the agent writes code, validates it, and improves without you relaying errors.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Your agent will make mistakes... The only question is, does it have the right leverage it needs to correct the mistakes?... You can create self-validating loops. These are called closed loop structures... If you're not writing tests, you're probably vibe coding."
core_concepts.misconception: Human-in-the-middle testing: running tests yourself and telling the agent what failed throws away the leverage. The loop closes only when the AGENT runs tests and reads results. Backends first (easiest, highest leverage); tests + stdout are the first two levers to install.

core_concepts.name: The abstraction ladder: plans → templates → ADWs
core_concepts.plain_english: Plans communicate massive batches of work (the 749-line spec bootstrapped this whole app — and Dan didn't type it; lesson 3 teaches planning with your agent). Templates are reusable agentic prompts committed to .claude/commands/ — mint one whenever you repeat a workflow three times (Dan creates /start on camera). ADWs top the ladder: agentic prompts + arbitrary code + an autonomous trigger, seeded by programmable mode (claude -p "/tools").
core_concepts.dan_words: "Put simply, plans are just prompts. Put accurately, plans are how you communicate massive amounts of work to your agent... Three time makes a pattern... Automate... ADWs are created when you combine one or more agentic prompts right out of the commands directory and then you wrap it in arbitrary code and then you kick it off autonomously with a trigger."
core_concepts.misconception: Ladder inversions: hand-typing plans; hoarding one-off prompts outside the repo; or chasing ADWs before single-prompt mastery — 'we must know how to fire off a single powerful agent running a single prompt... Master the primitives and you'll master the compositions.'

core_concepts.name: Four KPIs + the phase-one confession
core_concepts.plain_english: Track exactly four numbers — size (up), attempts (down toward 1), streak (up), presence (down toward 0) — and diagnose every failure back to a missing leverage point. Then the reveal: the whole lesson was Claude Code in 'phase one mode' (iterative back-and-forth), which tanks presence; from lesson 3 on, TAC shifts to programmable mode and the uncomfortable discipline of letting go of control.
core_concepts.dan_words: "If you don't measure it, you can't improve it... We have size, attempts, we have streak, and we have presence. This is it. This is all we need to track to win... We've been using Claude Code in phase one mode... This tanks our presence KPI... In order to let our code base run itself, we have to let go of control."
core_concepts.misconception: Reading 'iteration is bad' as absolute (exploratory iteration is fine; attempts rise temporarily when size scales — the sin is accepting iteration as the permanent workflow), or mistaking presence for productivity (feeling productive BECAUSE you watch every token is the early-game trap).

core_four.context: Everything in the context window: system prompts and conversation history per the slide. Through-agent levers work precisely because they 'typically flow through the context window' — stdout, test output, docs, plans all become context.
core_four.model: LLM selection and configuration. Barely dwelt on this lesson: 'reliable tool calling, agentic behavior and intelligence are no longer limitations thanks to modern LLMs and agents like Claude Code.'
core_four.prompt: User instructions and queries. This lesson's prompts are deliberately small (two-line fixes, slash commands) because the heavy lifting moves into through-agent levers; lesson 3 scales prompts into plans.
core_four.tools: Available functions and capabilities — introspectable via /tools since they're embedded in the system prompt. The Bash timeout parameter is the lesson's proof that tool-definition literacy pays: it enables running the app server inside the agent.
core_four.why_scale_matters: The core four are re-framed as the IN-AGENT half of the leverage-point taxonomy: 'your agent needs YOUR context, YOUR model, YOUR prompt, and YOUR tools.' Adopting the agent's perspective means auditing all four before every launch — the tactic card's litmus question — because they're always present whether you attend to them or not.

stdout_demo.before_summary: Committed repo state: app/server/server.py has six endpoints and zero print() calls; every handler catches exceptions and returns them as response-model error fields. The browser shows 'Error converting CSV to SQLite: near "(": syntax error' when orders_(32).csv is uploaded, but the server terminal shows nothing. Root cause is planted: server.py:60 derives the table name replacing only spaces, so parentheses survive; file_processor.py:26 then runs PRAGMA table_info(orders_(32)) — invalid SQLite.
stdout_demo.after_summary: Agent-performed fixes (NOT committed — the student reproduces them): (1) [ERROR] prints with full tracebacks + [SUCCESS] prints before every return across all endpoints ('Updated server.py to print detailed exception information and successful response details for all endpoints'); (2) sanitize_table_name() in core/file_processor.py (21 additions: strip extension, re.sub non-alphanumerics to underscores, ensure leading letter/underscore, never empty). After restart: upload succeeds, 'latest delivery' query works.
stdout_demo.difference_that_matters: Same bug, same agent — the only change between 'agent can't help here at all' and a two-prompt fix ('any issues with the server?' → 'resolve: replace bad chars and escape') is stdout visibility plus running the server inside the agent (Bash timeout 300s). The leverage point, not the model, was the bottleneck. This is Tactic #2 made operational: the litmus question failed, the system was upgraded, then it passed.

programmable_agent.why_it_matters: ADWs — the 12th leverage point and the course's destination — need agents callable from code. The lesson seeds this with claude -p "/tools": 'This is programmable mode. We're running this right from the terminal, not in iterative mode... do this work, call this command, whatever happens, return the result.' Slash commands compose: the same reusable prompts fired interactively all lesson run headlessly under -p, ready to be wrapped in arbitrary code and triggered autonomously.
languages: shell (claude -p invocation only in this lesson)

loot_box_mentions: Lesson 2 ships 18 loot notes; Dan points at the loot box twice on-camera: the tac-2 clone link ('link available in your loot box below if you wanna follow along') and the codebase-architecture checklist ('a concise list in your loot box below').

Idea notes distilling the lesson: Phase 2 SDLC (plan/code/test/review/document); the 12 leverage points; Tactic #2 adopt your agent's perspective; always think from agent's perspective; two types of leverage points (in-agent/through-agent); the core four; context = what can your agent see; documentation as agent-specific context; types as structured information; architecture as code-based navigation; tests = validation and self-correction; planning as meta-work; ADWs; agentic coding KPIs; one-shot success; mastering all 12; transition from AI coding to agentic coding.
step_by_step_demo: (5:52–6:15) Terminal: clone tac-2 (loot box link), open in VS Code, boot Claude Code — 'lean on our agent as the primary interface in which we do engineering work.'

(6:26–7:20) Type /install — a custom slash command (reusable prompt). install.md is 7 lines: it reads-and-executes prime.md ('running prompts inside of prompts... no different than passing a function inside of a function') then installs FE + BE deps (npm install; uv sync — the agent even self-corrects from a failed pip attempt to uv per the README).
(7:25–7:55) README step 2: cd app/server; cp .env.sample .env; add OPENAI_API_KEY and/or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ('make sure you don't leak this to anyone').
(7:55–8:15) ./scripts/start.sh in a fresh terminal (WSL if Windows) — backend :8000, frontend :5173, Ctrl+C cleanup.

(8:15–8:50) App tour: Upload Data → sample products.csv → in-memory-style SQLite table; query 'list top 5 products by price' → generated SQL (SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5;) + results table. 'A simple, beautiful, classic language model application.'

(9:30–10:45) /tools → the Core Tools list (Task, Bash w/ timeout, Glob, Grep, LS, Read, Edit, MultiEdit, Write; NotebookRead/Edit, WebFetch, WebSearch; TodoRead/TodoWrite; exit_plan_mode). Bash-timeout 'secret' flagged for later. MCP teaser.
(11:30–12:30) Drag orders_(32).csv into the app → browser error 'Error converting CSV to SQLite: near "(": syntax error'; server terminal silent → 'bad agentic code.'

(12:30–13:50) New agent; /prime; '@app/server/server.py — make sure every exception prints all exception details, every successful response prints before returning'; YOLO/auto-accept mode; review the [ERROR]/[SUCCESS] diff.
(13:50–14:30) Restart services; re-upload; the error now traces to server stdout. 'We're updating our codebase to communicate information to our agent.'

(14:30–15:50) Fresh agent; /prime; prompt: sh ./scripts/start.sh, 300s — the start script runs INSIDE the agent (Bash timeout param); reproduce the upload error; the agent has seen server + client stdout.

(15:50–16:30) Stop the run; prompt 'any issues with the server?' → agent diagnoses: SQL syntax error at app/server/core/file_processor.py:26, PRAGMA table_info({table_name}), unsanitized parentheses from uploaded filenames. Prompt 'resolve: replace bad chars and escape' → sanitize_table_name() added (21 additions).
(17:50–18:15) Up-arrow to relaunch inside the agent; delete the old db file; re-upload orders_(32).csv → success; query 'latest delivery' → correct rows.

(18:40–20:25) Types demo: open core/data_models.py, copy DatabaseSchemaResponse; brand-new Claude instance (zero context, on purpose); prompt 'show me how this type flows throughout the application, detail functions, files, and purpose' + format sketch; Task subagent runs (7 tool uses · 26.7k tokens · 59.2s) → five-file flow: data_models.py → server.py → types.d.ts → api/client.ts → specs/init_nlq_to_sql_to_table.md.
(21:05–21:30) Architecture: app/ splits client|server — 'cuts all of its work in half.'
(22:45–23:00) Copy prime.md's command into a bare terminal (git ls-files) to 'see what our agent sees' — a high-level map, but only a starting point.
(25:35–25:55) Tests mirror source: app/server/tests/core mirrors app/server/core.
(28:10–28:35) ! (bash mode): cd app/server; uv run pytest — all tests pass, full output lands in the agent's context.
(29:50–30:30) Open specs/init_nlq_to_sql_to_table.md — 749 lines of plan ('no way that I sat here and typed out 700 lines').
(32:25–32:55) Close the agent; claude -p "/tools" from the shell — programmable mode; result returns to the terminal. 'This is what we're gonna be doing inside of ADWs.'
(34:00–34:30) Crack open a markdown file: Four KPIs — Size / Attempts / Streak / Presence.
(42:10–42:55) Three-time rule payoff: create .claude/commands/start.md containing 'sh ./scripts/start.sh 300s'; boot claude; /start → server runs inside the agent on demand.

quotes.text: In lesson one, we set the stage. In lesson two, we start performing.

Just like with AI coding, Agentic Coding is easy to start, hard to master. All the low hanging fruit is getting chewed up. It's time to do the smart work, not the hard work, to get asymmetric return on your engineering.
If you pay attention, you can see the aspects that never change and you can place big bets on them.
Plan, code, test, review, document.
We're not here to write bigger prompts and iterate back and forth and back and forth. We're here to dial up the autonomy knob all the way to 11.
Adopt your agent's perspective.
Your agent is brilliant, but blind.
Agents are ephemeral, no context, no memories, and no awareness outside of what you give it. And when all the work is done, it resets back to zero.
Your agent needs your context, your model, your prompt, and your tools — the core four.
It's not about what you can do anymore. It's about what you can teach your agents to do.
We want the longest hot streak possible of success. When you stack up these leverage points, Agentic Coding success becomes inevitable.
Your agent can only see what you let it see.
Not only do we have bad code, we have bad agentic code.
I'm not actually fixing the issue. I'm setting up my codebase so that my agent can resolve the issue.
Types tell a story about how information travels throughout your codebase.
Types are IDKs — information dense keywords. They point to exact locations in your code base and represent the flow of a specific type of information.
If it's hard for you, you should assume it'll be hard for your agent.
Consistency is a powerful actor against complexity for both humans and for agents.
It's so important and widespread that I've called this the agent navigation problem.
Your agent will make mistakes, okay, just like you... The only question is, does it have the right leverage it needs to correct the mistakes?
If you're not writing tests, you're probably vibe coding.
Put simply, plans are just prompts. Put accurately, plans are how you communicate massive amounts of work to your agent.
The plan is the prompt, and that means great planning is great prompting.
ADWs are created when you combine one or more agentic prompts right out of the commands directory and then you wrap it in arbitrary code and then you kick it off autonomously with a trigger.
If you don't measure it, you can't improve it.
We're not aiming to become a babysitter for AI agents. We're looking for one shot solutions.
Once you start one-shotting, don't break the streak.
This is not the end game. This is the early game.
Are you still manually looking at error messages? Stop. Stop.
Three time makes a pattern. Three time should trigger your engineering brain. Automate.
It's not about you anymore. It's about what you can do for your agent so they can work for you.
English is the new programming language.
Master the primitives and you'll master the compositions.

prerequisites_tools: Everything from TAC-1 (terminal/WSL, git, Python + UV, Node.js + npm, IDE, Claude Code with plan or API funds)
OpenAI API key and/or Anthropic API key — first lesson where the DEMO APP itself calls LLM APIs (app/server/.env from .env.sample; at least one key required)
Python 3.10+ per pyproject (README troubleshooting says 3.12+; Dan's recording ran CPython 3.12.8)
A browser for localhost:5173 (frontend) / localhost:8000 (backend, /docs for API)
what_student_must_internalize: The 12 = core four IN the agent (context, model, prompt, tools) + 8 THROUGH the agent (standard out, types, documentation, tests, architecture, plans, templates, ADWs); through-agent levers work by flowing into the context window.
Tactic #2's litmus question, asked before every launch: with my agent's core four, is it possible to complete the task I've given it?
Agents are ephemeral — brilliant but blind, reset to zero every session; /prime and CLAUDE.md-style docs exist because of this, not as ritual.
Stdout is the agent's eyes on runtime behavior. Silent failure = bad agentic code even when the human-facing UX degrades gracefully.
Set up the system so the agent can fix the bug — don't fix the bug. Stop manually reading error messages; dig in only when your agent fails.
Types are IDKs: precise, searchable names create traceable information flows (model → endpoint → TS mirror → client → spec) that agents follow to do real work.
Architecture is a multiplier paid on every agent boot (the agent navigation problem); consistency is the antidote — but don't refactor yet, later lessons do it with your agent.
Tests + stdout are the first two levers to install: they create closed-loop structures where agents self-validate. No tests ≈ vibe coding.
The abstraction ladder: plans communicate massive work (plans are prompts), templates make prompts reusable (three-time rule → slash command), ADWs = prompts + code + trigger running autonomously.
Measure or you're guessing: size ↑, attempts ↓ (toward 1), streak ↑, presence ↓ (toward 0) — and every KPI miss maps back to a missing leverage point.
This lesson's own workflow was 'phase one mode' — iterative prompting that tanks presence; the course now shifts toward programmable mode and letting go of hands-on control.
common_weak_student_failures: Recites the 12 points but can't run the diagnostic — never answers 'which leverage point was missing?' when a run fails or a streak breaks.
Adds logging for humans (UI toasts, pretty dashboards) instead of stdout the agent process can actually read — then concludes the agent 'can't debug.'
Hand-fixes the planted orders_(32).csv bug in thirty seconds, ships a working app, and misses the entire point of the lesson's centerpiece demo.
Prompts 'fix the CSV bug' before adding stdout, watches the agent flail, and blames the model instead of the missing lever.
Skips /prime (or expects memory across sessions), then wonders why the agent doesn't 'know' the codebase it knew an hour ago.
Names things data/request/util/helper — generic words that make type-search useless ('it's cooked') and kill the IDK lever.
Runs pytest in their own terminal and pastes failures to the agent — a human-in-the-middle loop that forfeits self-validation.
Hears the architecture sermon and immediately hand-refactors the whole repo despite Dan's explicit 'don't refactor yet.'
Never mints slash commands (repeats the same start-the-server prompt for the tenth time) — the three-time rule exists to catch exactly this.
Treats KPIs as vibes: tracks nothing, so 'improving' is a feeling instead of size/attempts/streak/presence moving the right way.
teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) the two families of leverage points and all 12 members, and why 'through-agent' levers all route through the context window; (2) the stdout demo end-to-end — what made the server bad agentic code, why Dan refused to fix the bug directly, what 'sh ./scripts/start.sh, 300s' exploited, and the two short prompts that fixed it; (3) the four KPIs with directions, and how a broken streak turns into a leverage-point diagnosis; and (4) the tactic that summarizes it all — adopt your agent's perspective — including its litmus question. Finish with the lesson's closing paradox: why does dropping YOUR presence (letting go of control) increase what gets engineered?

retrieval_questions.q: Name the two families of leverage points and all 12 members.
retrieval_questions.a: In-agent (core four): context, model, prompt, tools. Through-agent: standard out, types, documentation, tests, architecture, plans, templates, ADWs.

retrieval_questions.q: State Tactic #2 and its litmus question.
retrieval_questions.a: Adopt your agent's perspective. Before every launch: 'With my agent's core four (context, model, prompt, tools), is it possible to complete the task I've given it?'

retrieval_questions.q: What are the five steps of the phase-two SDLC, and why bet on the SDLC at all?
retrieval_questions.a: Plan, code, test, review, document — the SDLC is an aspect of engineering that never changes, so it survives tool/model churn.

retrieval_questions.q: Why was the demo server 'bad agentic code,' and what exactly was the planted bug?
retrieval_questions.a: Every endpoint swallowed exceptions into response error fields with zero stdout, so agents couldn't see failures. The upload path only replaces spaces when deriving table names, so orders_(32).csv → table orders_(32) → PRAGMA table_info fails at file_processor.py:26 with an SQLite syntax error near '('.

retrieval_questions.q: What command ran the app inside the agent, and which tool detail made it possible?
retrieval_questions.a: sh ./scripts/start.sh, 300s — exploiting the Bash tool's timeout parameter Dan surfaced by reading /tools output.

retrieval_questions.q: Reproduce Dan's two bug-fixing prompts and say why they sufficed.
retrieval_questions.a: 'Any issues with the server?' then 'resolve: replace bad chars and escape.' They sufficed because the system had been set up first: stdout logging everywhere + the server running inside the agent's context.

retrieval_questions.q: What does IDK stand for, and through which five files does DatabaseSchemaResponse flow?
retrieval_questions.a: Information dense keywords. core/data_models.py → server.py → client/src/types.d.ts → client/src/api/client.ts → specs/init_nlq_to_sql_to_table.md.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the agent navigation problem and its antidote?
retrieval_questions.a: Every fresh agent boot must re-explore the codebase (hundreds/thousands of times), so structure compounds for or against you; the antidote is consistency — same patterns, folder structures, function/file names, comment structure.

retrieval_questions.q: List five items from Dan's codebase-architecture checklist.
retrieval_questions.a: Any five of: clear entry points; constant files for unchanging info; types/classes/structures; meaningful verbose IDK names; files under ~1000 lines; agent-facing markdown (README/CLAUDE.md) throughout the tree; separated services; one responsibility per file; tests mirroring source structure.

retrieval_questions.q: What are the two types of documentation, and what is ai_docs/ for?
retrieval_questions.a: Internal (codebase docs like README/CLAUDE.md) and external (third-party). ai_docs/ is a dedicated agent-facing folder of local external docs so agents don't make web requests every lookup.

retrieval_questions.q: What are closed-loop structures, and what's the vibe-coding line?
retrieval_questions.a: Structures where the agent gets a concrete feedback loop to validate its own work (e.g., running tests whose output hits stdout). 'If you're not writing tests, you're probably vibe coding.'

retrieval_questions.q: Give both formulations of 'plans' and the spec fact that proves the point.
retrieval_questions.a: Put simply: plans are just prompts. Put accurately: plans are how you communicate massive amounts of work to your agent. specs/init_nlq_to_sql_to_table.md is 749 lines — and Dan didn't hand-type it.

retrieval_questions.q: Define an ADW precisely, and name the mode that seeds it.
retrieval_questions.a: One or more agentic prompts (from the commands directory) wrapped in arbitrary code, kicked off autonomously with a trigger. Seeded by programmable mode: claude -p "/tools" — run headlessly, return the result.

retrieval_questions.q: Name the four KPIs with directions and Dan's streak math.
retrieval_questions.a: Size up, attempts down (toward one per prompt), streak up, presence down (toward zero). Five one-shot prompts vs five prompts with three fixes each: the fixer is 3x slower.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the three-time rule, and what command did Dan mint with it?
retrieval_questions.a: 'Three time makes a pattern. Three time should trigger your engineering brain: automate.' He created .claude/commands/start.md containing 'sh ./scripts/start.sh 300s' → /start.

retrieval_questions.q: What confession ends the lesson, and what changes going forward?
retrieval_questions.a: The whole lesson used Claude Code in phase-one (iterative) mode, which tanks the presence KPI; from here TAC shifts to programmable mode — letting go of hands-on control while keeping observability.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Reusable prompts (.claude/commands) → Agent Skills + richer command syntax
current_practice_gaps.why: tac-2's templates leverage point is proto-Skills: bare markdown prompts fired by name. Current Claude Code adds first-class Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter, trigger descriptions, on-demand loading, bundled scripts/resources) plus upgraded slash commands ($ARGUMENTS, frontmatter like allowed-tools, project/user scoping). The concept maps 1:1 — 'reusable, embeddable, agentic prompts' — the packaging and discovery upgraded.

current_practice_gaps.gap: The /tools output is a period snapshot of Claude Code's toolset
current_practice_gaps.why: The on-screen list (Task-as-search-subagent, TodoRead/TodoWrite, exit_plan_mode, MultiEdit, NotebookRead/Edit) reflects course-era Claude Code. Current builds rename/reshape tools (typed subagents, task tools, background Bash + BashOutput, SlashCommand/Skill invocation, AskUserQuestion, plan-mode changes) and auto-truncate giant stdout. The lesson's HABIT — introspect the tool surface, read parameter definitions, exploit details like Bash timeout — transfers unchanged; the exact roster is period detail.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Running servers inside the agent: fixed Bash timeout → background tasks
current_practice_gaps.why: Dan's 'sh ./scripts/start.sh, 300s' blocks a foreground Bash call for up to five minutes — clever for its era. Current Claude Code runs long-lived processes as background tasks whose output the agent polls on demand, so a server can run indefinitely while the agent keeps working. Same leverage point (agent sees runtime stdout), sturdier machinery.

current_practice_gaps.gap: No CLAUDE.md committed; agent-docs conventions have since standardized
current_practice_gaps.why: Dan verbally credits 'the claude.md' alongside /prime, but tac-2 ships none — README + prime carry the role. Current practice: a root CLAUDE.md (and nested ones for subsystems, plus AGENTS.md interop) auto-loaded per session, bootstrapped by /init, layered user/project/local. The lesson's principle — distributed agent-facing docs — is now paved-road tooling.

current_practice_gaps.gap: YOLO mode / permissions: auto-accept edits → modes, hooks, sandboxing
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson toggles auto-accept ('yolo mode') and ships a flat allow/deny settings.json (already ahead of tac-1 by including deny rules for git push --force and rm -rf). Current Claude Code offers permission modes (plan / acceptEdits / bypassPermissions), pre/post tool-use hooks, and sandboxed execution — teams gate autonomy with policy rather than a single toggle. The deny-list instinct the repo models is exactly where practice went.

current_practice_gaps.gap: KPIs remain manual; the ecosystem now has measurable proxies
current_practice_gaps.why: Dan says systematize size/attempts/streak/presence 'inside GitHub or Jira or whatever you want to use' — in-course it's a markdown file and mental tracking. Current tooling (session logs, OTEL metrics, cost/usage dashboards, PR-per-agent-run workflows) can quantify run duration (size), retry counts (attempts), consecutive green runs (streak), and human-interaction counts (presence). The metrics were ahead of their tooling; the definitions still hold.

setup: Clone the course repo: git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-2.git && cd tac-2 (or use the local codebase/ symlink → tac/tac-2)
Read .claude/settings.json aloud: which nine Bash patterns + Write are allowed, and which three commands are DENIED (git push --force, git push -f, rm -rf) — first TAC repo with a deny list
cd app/server && cp .env.sample .env; add OPENAI_API_KEY and/or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (at least one — the app itself calls LLMs)
Boot claude in the repo; run /install (watch install.md read-and-execute prime.md — prompts inside prompts); alternatively uv sync --all-extras + npm install manually
./scripts/start.sh from a fresh terminal; verify localhost:5173 loads and localhost:8000/docs answers; upload sample products.csv and run 'list top 5 products by price'
reproduce_dan: Break it: drag app/client/public/sample-data/orders_(32).csv into Upload Data; capture the browser error AND confirm the server terminal printed nothing (the bad-agentic-code state)

Install the stdout lever: new agent → /prime → '@app/server/server.py make sure every exception prints all exception details, and every successful response prints before returning' (auto-accept on); verify the [ERROR]/[SUCCESS] diff
Prove visibility: restart services, re-upload the bad CSV, confirm the SQLite error now traces to the server's stdout
Run the app INSIDE the agent: fresh agent → /prime → prompt exactly: sh ./scripts/start.sh, 300s — then reproduce the upload error in the browser

The two-prompt fix: ask 'any issues with the server?' (expect a diagnosis naming core/file_processor.py:26 and unescaped special characters), then 'resolve: replace bad chars and escape'; review the sanitize_table_name diff
Close the loop: relaunch, delete the old db file, re-upload orders_(32).csv (should succeed with a sanitized table name), and query 'latest delivery' — verify sensible rows

Types drill: copy DatabaseSchemaResponse from core/data_models.py; open a BRAND-NEW claude instance; prompt 'show me how this type flows throughout the application, detail functions, files, and purpose' with a format sketch; verify its answer against reality (grep -rn DatabaseSchemaResponse → data_models.py / server.py / types.d.ts / api/client.ts / the spec)

Tests drill: inside the agent, ! then cd app/server && uv run pytest — all tests pass with output in-context; then ask the agent to add a test for sanitize_table_name covering parenthesized filenames and run it (closed loop)

Templates drill: after your third manual server-start, mint the command Dan mints: create .claude/commands/start.md containing 'sh ./scripts/start.sh 300s'; restart claude; verify /start boots both services inside the agent
ADW seed: from a plain shell, run claude -p "/tools" and watch the reusable prompt execute headlessly and return
stretch: S1 — Prime upgrade: extend .claude/commands/prime.md (via the agent) to also read core/data_models.py; boot a fresh agent, /prime, and compare how much less exploration the type questions need

S2 — Leverage-point ablation: revert the stdout prints (git checkout app/server/server.py), keep sanitize_table_name reverted too, and ask a fresh agent to 'fix the CSV upload bug' with NO stdout and the server running OUTSIDE the agent; document the flailing, then restore the levers and repeat — write one sentence on what changed (this is the 12-points diagnostic, experienced)

S3 — KPI journal: for your next three agentic prompts in this repo, log size (minutes of agent run), attempts (post-completion corrections), streak (consecutive one-shots), presence (times you intervened); when a one-shot fails, name the missing leverage point in writing

S4 — IDK audit: pick the worst-named type/function in a codebase you own; list the places an agent would have to search to trace it; rename it to an information-dense keyword (with your agent) and re-run the trace prompt

S5 — Architecture checklist sweep: score tac-2 against all nine checklist items (entry points, constants, types, verbose names, file size, distributed docs, separated services, one-responsibility files, mirrored tests) — then score one of YOUR repos; do NOT refactor yet, just write the gap list (Dan: don't refactor yet)
pass_criteria: Zero hand-typed application code: every code change in the lab (prints, sanitize_table_name, prime.md edit, start.md) was written by the agent
Browser upload of orders_(32).csv fails with a syntax error BEFORE the fixes and succeeds AFTER, with the server's stdout showing [ERROR]/[SUCCESS] traces you can point to
The agent's diagnosis run cited the real failing file/line (core/file_processor.py PRAGMA call) from stdout it observed itself — you did not paste the error to it
Type-flow answer names all five real locations of DatabaseSchemaResponse, cross-checked by your own grep
uv run pytest executed INSIDE the agent with all tests passing, including a new agent-written sanitize test
/start works from a fresh claude session, and claude -p "/tools" returns the tool list headlessly

Closing oral check, no notes: the 12 points in two families; Tactic #2 + litmus question; the four KPIs with directions; which leverage point you'd reach for first in a codebase with silent failures (stdout) and which right after (tests)
